quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
quiz_item.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

pamphlet_excerpts: Elevation Above Sea Level: Using a Topographic Map. maps you will find a number on it that tells its elevation abovesea level (p. 14).
Thick Index Contour Lines: On orienteering maps, the index contour line does not have an elevation number, but is thicker than the others and is used as a guide for the eye (p. 14).
Visualizing Terrain From Contours: You can also "see" the shape of the terrain from the profile of the lines on the paper (p. 14).
Conical Mountain Contour Rings: If a mountain is perfectly conical like a wizard's hat, the contour lines depicting the mountain will look like a bull's-eye (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Read Terrain Line Profiles: You can also "see" the shape of the terrain from the profile of the lines on the paper (p. 14).
Step 2 - Identify Concentric Peak Contours: If a mountain is perfectly conical like a wizard's hat, the contour lines depicting the mountain will look like a bull's-eye (p. 14).
Step 3 - Check Equal Contour Spacing: Each contour line will be perfectly circular, and all will be the same distance apart (p. 14).
Step 4 - Spot Valleys and Depressions: At one part of the mountain, the contour line may intersect a valley or a depression (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: Aligning the Compass Bezel: Rotate the bezel until the orienting arrow or north-south lines lie parallel to and in the same direction as the magnetic north-south lines on the map (p. 10).
Reading the Bearing Index: Read the bearing directly opposite of the bearing index (p. 10).
Converting Map and Compass: If the magnetic north-south lines are not drawn on the map, convert the language of the compass to that of the map (p. 10).
Adjusting for Magnetic Declination: Always add the number of degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Convert Map Compass Angles: If the magnetic north-south lines are not drawn on the map, convert the language of the compass to that of the map (p. 10).
Step 2 - Add or Subtract Declination: Always add the number of degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).
Step 3 - Read Exact Degree Bearings: The bearing is 244 degrees from "A" to "B." (Points "A" and "B" can be seen in the top photo on page 21.) (p. 10).
Step 4 - Navigate With Thumb Compasses: The thumb compass rides on the thumb and simplifies map orientation and direction finding while you are on the move (p. 10).

pamphlet_excerpts: Meaning of Map Orientation: Using a Map and Compass Together Orienting a Map With a Compass Orienting a map means aligning it with the terrain (p. 19).
Limits of Visual Alignment: You can do this visually, but it is easier to make errors that way (p. 19).
Precision of Compass Alignment: A more accurate way of aligning the map and terrain is to use a compass (p. 19).
Setting Bezel to North: First, rotate the compass bezel until Nor 360 degrees is lined up with the direction-of-travel arrow (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Choose Compass Over Sight: A more accurate way of aligning the map and terrain is to use a compass (p. 19).
Step 2 - Set Bezel to North: First, rotate the compass bezel until Nor 360 degrees is lined up with the direction-of-travel arrow (p. 19).
Step 3 - Align Edge With Meridian: Next, set the compass down on the map, with the compass edge along one of the north-south magnetic lines and the direction-of-travel arrow pointing (p. 19).
Step 4 - Rotate Map and Compass: Rotate the map and the compass together until the compass needle matches the direction-of-travel arrow (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: Adjusting for Speed Changes: Every timeorienteers switch from walking to running or the reverse, they must mentally adjust the pace and time as well (p. 26).
Counting Paces and Time: Once you have laid out the course, start at the beginning and walk the length of it, counting the number of paces and recording the time it takes you to reach (p. 26).
Baseline Per Hundred Meters: This is your walking pace and time per 100 meters (p. 26).
Averaging Multiple Pace Trials: You will get a more accurate measure if you walk the course two or more times and then divide the total paces and minutes by the total meters walked (p. 26).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Record Hundred Meter Baseline: This is your walking pace and time per 100 meters (p. 26).
Step 2 - Average Multiple Course Runs: You will get a more accurate measure if you walk the course two or more times and then divide the total paces and minutes by the total meters walked (p. 26).
Step 3 - Account for Uneven Ground: This is particularly important if the course is on uneven ground (p. 26).
Step 4 - Measure Running Pace Speed: Judging Distance on the Ground Running Pace/Time Foot speed is important in orienteering, especially for competitive orienteering (p. 26).

pamphlet_excerpts: Turning at Linear Features: If you arrive at the linear feature and do not see the control, you will then know which way to turn to find (p. 38).
Avoiding Direction Uncertainty: In this map, it would be easy to reach the road and not be sure what direction the control lies (p. 38).
Deliberate Aiming Off Strategy: To prevent this, you can deliberately aim a few meters south of the control so you know to turn north when you get to the road (p. 38).
Mental Picture of Terrain: Keep a clear mental picture of the terrain that you will pass (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Aim Off to One Side: To prevent this, you can deliberately aim a few meters south of the control so you know to turn north when you get to the road (p. 38).
Step 2 - Visualize Upcoming Terrain Shapes: Keep a clear mental picture of the terrain that you will pass (p. 38).
Step 3 - Read Map Every Few Seconds: Read the map every few seconds, think beyond your location, and plan ahead (p. 38).
Step 4 - Plan Ahead After Controls: The best way to practice reading ahead is to take time at the beginning of the course and after each control to make sure you understand (p. 38).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: If your map does not have magnetic north-south lines drawn on it, how do you adjust a map bearing for magnetic declination?

C. Multiply the contour interval by the magnetic variation angle

choices: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): To convert from true north on the map to magnetic north on the compass, always add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).
